newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks to work with developers to save wildlife.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks to work with developers to save wildlife.

text.p: Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt Friday announced two proposals to expand the government's efforts with private landowners to help save endangered plants and animals.
The initiatives have been in the works for some time, but Babbitt and Commerce Secretary William Daley touted them to show that the Endangered Species Act was working.

Two years ago, House Republicans were intent on overhauling the law to ease restrictions on developers, but they have grown much quieter after suffering at the polls for their bids to roll back green protections.

The Clinton administration's initiatives would shield developers from tight restrictions on their land if they commit voluntarily to protecting or building up habitats that are essential for threatened species to survive.

Landowners have often avoided taking any steps to save endangered species on their property for fear that if the imperilled population increased, the government would later spring new restrictions on the landowners in line with the Endangered Species Act.

Under the proposed safe harbour agreements for endangered species and so-called candidate conservation agreements for species close to becoming listed, federal and state agencies would have to determine that a particular species would end up better off because of steps a landowner proposed to take.

The agencies would assure the landowner that if the imperilled population increased as a result of the landowner's voluntary activities, the landowner's property would not later be subject to any new regulations or restrictions.
An owner could then do anything he wanted with the land, as long as the species was not harmed in the long run.
Under a similar plan, the government is close to working out habitat conservation plans with owners of more than 18 million acres of land, protecting more than 300 species.

In a separate move designed to protect key habitats on public lands, the Nature Conservancy Friday signed an agreement with the Federal Highway Administration to work with the agency on road planning.

The environmental group said it would help the U.S. agency and state transportation departments collect information on imperilled plants and animals, then recommend the best routes to avoid fragile populations amid road work.

Under one such project which the broad agreement was intended to mirror, road builders saved a rare salamander that lived on a rock face that was to be blasted to widen a federal highway in Montana, by removing the creatures before the rock was destroyed and returning them after the work was completed.
